meta.description: Ira Hayes really said it — but at a Boston rally reported 14 May 1945, not to President Truman. The paper printed “How can I,” not “How could I.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'How Could I Feel Like a Hero When Only Five Men in My Platoon of 45 Survived?'?
meta.ogDescription: He said it — but not to Truman. The Boston Daily Globe of 14 May 1945 printed Ira Hayes's words at a Boston rally, verified on microfilm.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1923–1955 · Pima Marine, Iwo Jima flag raiser
answer.sourceLine: Hayes really said it — but at a rally in Boston, not in the White House. The Boston Daily Globe of 14 May 1945 printed the line in Hy Hurwitz’s report on three Iwo Jima flag raisers, a citation Quote Investigator ↗ had verified on microfilm. The paper’s wording begins “How can I feel like a hero” and ends as a statement, not a question.

source.heading: Where the line was actually said

docMeta.dd: Hub Throng Thrills 3 Iwo Heroes: Turnout in Rain Inspiring, Say Flag Raisers
Boston Daily Globe, 14 May 1945, p. 9, col. 7
Pfc. Ira Hayes, Company E, 2nd Battalion, 28th Marines

source.excerpt: But these men will never forget their many friends who will never enjoy the fruits of the victory. “How can I feel like a hero,” said Hayes, “when only five men in my platoon of 45 survived, when only 27 men in my company of 250 managed to escape death or injury.”
trail: 14 May 1945 — the Boston Daily Globe. Hy Hurwitz’s page-9 report on a Boston rally for three Iwo Jima flag raisers carries the line. Quote Investigator ↗ had the citation verified on microfilm by researcher Joel S. Berson, and treats it as the documented appearance of the quotation.

1995 — Shadow of Suribachi. Parker Bishop Albee Jr. and Keller Cushing Freeman’s study of the two flag raisings quotes the words and gives the precise 1945 Globe date; the Praeger edition is catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗.

The platoon figure is repeated elsewhere. Hayes was “one of five marines remaining from his original platoon of 45 men, including their corpsmen,” according to Wikipedia’s account of his Iwo Jima service ↗ — though that account descends from Hayes’s own 1945 statements, so it repeats the figure rather than independently checking it. The second half of the quotation — 27 men out of a company of 250 — has no separate corroborating source here.

1999–2005 — the drift. John Updike changed “can” to “could” and set the line beside the 1954 monument dedication; by 2005 a newspaper column had Hayes saying it to President Truman. Both steps are documented at Quote Investigator ↗.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed by Quote Investigator from microfilm. QI flags one printing error in the original: where this transcription reads “death or injury,” the newspaper text has “of.” The three flag raisers at the rally were Rene Gagnon of Manchester, New Hampshire; Ira “The Chief” Hayes of Bapchule, Arizona; and John Bradley of Appleton, Wisconsin.

source.rightsNote: The line survives because a reporter wrote it down, so the rights question attaches to his article: Hy Hurwitz’s report in the Boston Daily Globe of 14 May 1945. As a work first published well after 1930 by an identifiable newspaper, it is treated here as in copyright to the Globe and its successors. Hayes’s spoken words have no separate publication of their own, and the renewal status of this particular 1945 issue has not been checked — so the conservative classification stands.

author.name: Ira Hayes
author.heading: Ira Hayes
author.metaLine: 1923–1955 · U.S. Marine, Gila River Pima, Iwo Jima flag raiser
author.bio: Ira Hamilton Hayes was born on 12 January 1923 in Sacaton, Arizona, an enrolled member of the Gila River Indian Community, and enlisted in the Marine Corps Reserve in August 1942 — becoming, by Wikipedia’s account, the first Pima to receive his paratrooper wings. He fought on Bougainville and then on Iwo Jima with Company E, 2nd Battalion, 28th Marines, and was one of the six men who raised the second flag on Mount Suribachi on 23 February 1945. Fame was the part he could not survive: pulled home to sell war bonds, he spent the next decade refusing the word “hero,” and was found dead near Sacaton on 24 January 1955.

copyAttribution: "How can I feel like a hero, when only five men in my platoon of 45 survived, when only 27 men in my company of 250 managed to escape death or injury." —Ira Hayes, at a Boston rally, reported by Hy Hurwitz, Boston Daily Globe, 14 May 1945, p. 9. Not, as commonly claimed, said to President Truman at the White House.

misattribution.heading: Right man, wrong room
misattribution.intro: This is an unusual case for a famous-name quotation: the words are genuine and contemporaneously documented. It is the scene that was invented, and a single auxiliary verb that was changed along the way.

items.who: President Harry Truman, at the White House
items.why: A 2005 Long Beach Press-Telegram column framed the line as Hayes’s answer when Truman called him a hero, and that version now dominates retellings. Quote Investigator ↗ found no source placing the words there. The confusion has a real hook: Hayes, Gagnon and Bradley did meet Truman at the White House on 20 April 1945, per Wikipedia’s chronology ↗ — just not to say this.

Other accounts move the line to the dedication of the Marine Corps War Memorial on 10 November 1954, where Hayes met President Eisenhower, per Wikipedia ↗. Quote Investigator ↗ suggests these versions may rest on a misreading of John Updike’s 1999 essay — or, in QI’s own hedge, of “some other similarly compact account” — the essay interweaving the quotation, Hayes’s “good buddies” remark and the 1954 ceremony in one compressed paragraph.

items.who: “How could I feel like a hero…?”
items.why: The wording that circulates today — “could,” with the numbers spelled out and a question mark at the end — is Updike’s 1999 rendering, not the newspaper’s. The Globe printed “How can I feel like a hero,” and set it as a statement. Both forms are laid side by side at Quote Investigator ↗.

James Bradley and Ron Powers print a shorter version that keeps only the company arithmetic — 250 buddies, 27 walking off alive — and drops the platoon figures. Quote Investigator ↗ notes the book gives no citation for it; the Bantam edition is catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Hayes’s, and a reporter wrote them down in the spring of 1945 — at a Boston rally, in Hy Hurwitz’s report in the Boston Daily Globe of 14 May 1945, and not to a president in the White House. Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: Why he answered with a casualty return
lead: Hayes helped raise the second flag on Mount Suribachi on 23 February 1945 and left the island with his unit on 27 March. Of the 45 men in his original platoon, he was one of five still standing. Within weeks he had been pulled out of the Pacific and sent home to sell war bonds on the Seventh War Loan drive, appearing alongside Rene Gagnon and John Bradley in front of crowds who wanted to call all three of them heroes.

So when a Boston crowd turned out in the rain and a Globe reporter asked how it felt, the answer Hayes gave was not modesty. It was a casualty return, delivered in numbers. What later writers did was move it — first into a tighter narrative that sat the line beside the 1954 monument dedication, and eventually into a White House scene with President Truman that no contemporary source records.
detailsBody: 1995 — Shadow of Suribachi. Parker Bishop Albee Jr. and Keller Cushing Freeman quote the line essentially as the Globe printed it and give the precise 1945 newspaper date, framing it as evidence that Hayes genuinely refused the title of hero.

1999 — John Updike. In ‘Descent of an Image’ (More Matter, Knopf), Updike switches “can” to “could”, spells the numbers out in words, and runs the quotation together with Hayes’s “good buddies” remark and the 1954 Iwo Jima monument ceremony. Quote Investigator calls the passage tightly interwoven and suspects it seeded the later confusion.

2000 — Flags of Our Fathers. James Bradley and Ron Powers give a shorter version that keeps only the company arithmetic — 250 buddies, 27 walking off alive — and drops the platoon figures entirely. Quote Investigator notes the book supplies no citation for its wording.

2005 — the Truman version. A Long Beach Press-Telegram column presented the line as Hayes’s reply when Truman called him a hero. That is the framing that now dominates search results, and it is the one Quote Investigator set out to test — and could not support.
context.pull: The arithmetic was not rhetoric. His platoon came off Iwo Jima with five men left out of 45.

schema.claimQuoteText: How Could I Feel Like a Hero When Only Five Men in My Platoon of 45 Survived?
schema.claimReviewed: Ira Hayes said the line — at a Boston rally reported by Hy Hurwitz in the Boston Daily Globe of 14 May 1945, p. 9, col. 7, not to President Truman at the White House. The attribution is verified; the circulating wording is not. The Globe printed it as a statement, “How can I feel like a hero, when only five men in my platoon of 45 survived, when only 27 men in my company of 250 managed to escape death or injury.” The familiar “How could I feel like a hero…?” is John Updike’s 1999 rendering.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator identifies the Boston Daily Globe of 14 May 1945 — “Hub Throng Thrills 3 Iwo Heroes: Turnout in Rain Inspiring, Say Flag Raisers” by Hy Hurwitz, page 9, column 7, verified on microfilm by Joel S. Berson — as containing Hayes's words: “How can I feel like a hero, when only five men in my platoon of 45 survived, when only 27 men in my company of 250 managed to escape death or injury.” The event was a rally in Boston attended by Rene Gagnon, Ira Hayes and John Bradley, not a visit to the White House.

Quote Investigator reproduces a 24 February 2005 Long Beach Press-Telegram column by Tom Hennessy (page A2) that frames the line as Hayes's reply when Harry Truman called him a hero, and states that some later writers began claiming the quote was spoken at the White House or at the Iwo Jima monument dedication, possibly from misreading Updike.

Quote Investigator quotes John Updike's essay “Descent of an Image” (More Matter: Essays and Criticism, Alfred A. Knopf, 1999, page 678), which renders the line as “How could I feel like a hero…” with numbers spelled out, and interweaves it with the “good buddies” remark and the 1954 Iwo Jima monument dedication.

Quote Investigator quotes Flags of Our Fathers (James Bradley with Ron Powers, Bantam Books, 2000, page 12), whose shorter variant keeps only the 250/27 company figures and drops the platoon count, and notes that the book does not provide a citation.

Quote Investigator quotes Shadow of Suribachi by Parker Bishop Albee Jr. and Keller Cushing Freeman (Praeger, Westport, Connecticut, 1995, page 112), which presents the quotation and gives the precise date of its appearance in the Boston Daily Globe.
Quote Investigator states that the newspaper account contains a typo: the word “or” in its transcribed excerpt actually appears as “of” in the newspaper text.

Wikipedia states that after Iwo Jima, “Hayes was one of five marines remaining from his original platoon of 45 men, including their corpsmen,” and that he left Iwo Jima with his unit for Hawaii on 27 March 1945.
Wikipedia states that on 20 April 1945 Gagnon, Hayes and Bradley met President Truman at the White House, and that the three took part in the Seventh War Loan drive bond-selling tour.

Wikipedia gives Ira Hamilton Hayes's dates as 12 January 1923 – 24 January 1955, born in Sacaton, Arizona, an enrolled member of the Gila River Indian Community; records his service with Company E, 2nd Battalion, 28th Marines, 5th Marine Division; his participation in the second flag raising on Mount Suribachi on 23 February 1945; his promotion to corporal on 19 June 1945; and that he attended the Marine Corps War Memorial dedication on 10 November 1954, where he met President Dwight D. Eisenhower.

The National Museum of the Marine Corps biographical brief confirms Hayes was a Pima Native American and Gila River reservation member, enlisted in the Marine Corps Reserve in 1942, fought at Bougainville and Iwo Jima, participated in the Seventh War Loan Drive in 1945, and died on 24 January 1955 near Sacaton, Arizona.

The Internet Archive holds a catalogue record for “Shadow of Suribachi: Raising the Flags on Iwo Jima” by Parker Bishop Albee and Keller Cushing Freeman, published by Praeger, Westport, Conn., 1995 — matching the edition Quote Investigator cites.
The Internet Archive holds a scanned Bantam Books edition of “Flags of Our Fathers” by James Bradley with Ron Powers (access-restricted lending copy).
Negative check: Wikiquote has no page for Ira Hayes (HTTP 404), so there is no Wikiquote sourced, attributed or misattributed section for this line. No Wikiquote link is used on this page.
